Reviews · Lancia Delta HF Integrale Evoluzione · 1991–1994

The King Was Italian

The Golf GTI invented the hot hatch and the 205 GTI perfected it. Then Lancia took a boxy 1979 family car, bolted a turbo to it, drove all four wheels, and won six consecutive World Rally Championships — a record that in thirty-four years nothing has come close to touching.

By Douglas James · Carveyance · 26 min read

In 1995 a game arrived on the Sega Saturn that quietly recruited an entire generation into rallying, and it did it with exactly two cars.

Sega Rally Championship gave you a choice. Door number one: a Toyota Celica GT-Four in Castrol green and white. Door number two: a Lancia Delta HF Integrale in Martini stripes. Both rendered with the actual sponsor liveries, both detailed to a standard nobody expected from a console, both genuinely different to drive. Three stages — desert, forest, mountain — and if you took first in all three you earned a fourth. There was a Stratos hidden in there too, for anyone who went looking.

Everybody had a side. Mine was the Lancia. It handled better. It stuck to the ground harder. It gave you more control on the loose stuff and it sounded better doing it. That was not brand loyalty — I had no idea what a Lancia was. That was a fourteen-year-old discovering, through a $50 cartridge, that some cars are simply better at the job.

A year later I found out I had been right.

Section 01 — First contactHong Kong, 1996

I remember exactly where I was. Walking from the Rose Cliff apartments up to the American Club, ordinary afternoon, and a fire-engine-red Integrale pulled up alongside me. It must have just been washed. It was immaculate — that hard, wet-looking red that only ever seems to happen on Italian cars and only ever in the twenty minutes after a detail.

Then the light changed, traffic moved, and I heard it.

I have been genuinely moved by seeing a car maybe five or six times in my life. It happens less now than it did at fifteen, which I suspect is true for everyone. But that one landed and stayed landed, because of the order things happened in: I already knew what it was. I had spent an unreasonable number of hours inside a digital one. And then the real thing rolled up next to me in Hong Kong traffic, made a noise, and left.

Section 02 — The crownAbout the Golf, and about the 205

Ask the internet to name the king of hot hatches and it will say Golf GTI, which is defensible for the same reason people say the Wright brothers invented flight. The Mk1 GTI created the category out of nothing in 1976 and Volkswagen has been building the thing without interruption for fifty years. Longevity is an argument. Continuity is an argument.

The Peugeot 205 GTI deserves a deeper bow than it usually gets. It was lighter than the Golf, sharper than the Golf, funnier than the Golf, and it will still embarrass a modern hatchback on the right road. It also won two World Rally Championships in T16 form, which is more than the Golf can say. Full and genuine respect. Nobody who loves the 205 is wrong.

But here is the case, and it is not close.

A hot hatch is an ordinary car made extraordinary. By that definition the Integrale isn't just the best one ever built — it's the only one that went out and proved it against the entire industry, six years running, on ice and gravel and tarmac, in front of the world.The argument in one paragraph

The Golf GTI is the most successful hot hatch. The 205 GTI may be the most delightful. The Integrale is the most accomplished — and it is the only one of the three whose road-car specification exists because a rally team needed the parts approved.

Section 03 — The ordinary car underneathA 1979 family hatchback. Really.

Start where the legend starts, which is somewhere completely unglamorous.

The Lancia Delta appeared at the Frankfurt show in 1979: a Giorgetto Giugiaro design for Italdesign, five doors, front-wheel drive, transverse engine, upright glass, built on conventional mass-production tooling and sold as the sophisticated relation to Fiat's cheaper cars. It was comfortable and sensible and beautifully proportioned in a plain way. It won the 1980 European Car of the Year award. Between 1980 and 1982, Saab even sold a rebadged version in Scandinavia as the Saab-Lancia 600.

By the time the first generation finished in the mid-nineties, Lancia had built 478,645 of them. The overwhelming majority went to school runs.

This matters enormously, and it is the thing that separates the Integrale from the Stratos and the 037 and the Delta S4. Those were purpose-built weapons wearing production badges. The Integrale's roofline, doors, windshield, seating position and fundamental shell came from a car designed to carry groceries. Everything Lancia achieved, it achieved by modifying rather than replacing.

Section 04 — Why it existedGroup B dies, and Lancia already has the answer

Through the early eighties, rallying belonged to Group B: the Audi Quattro, the Peugeot 205 T16, Lancia's own 037 and Delta S4, the Ford RS200, the MG Metro 6R4. Space frames, silhouette bodies, in some cases both a supercharger and a turbocharger. The Delta S4 was called a Delta and looked vaguely like one, and was mechanically nothing of the sort.

After a run of fatal accidents the FIA killed Group B at the end of 1986. Group A — which demanded a genuine, volume-produced road car underneath — became the premier category for 1987, effective immediately.

Every manufacturer in the paddock now needed a compact, turbocharged, four-wheel-drive production car with five thousand examples on the road. Most of them had nothing. Lancia had launched the Delta HF 4WD in May 1986, roughly eight months before the rules changed, for reasons that had nothing to do with any of this.

It won the 1987 Monte Carlo Rally. The first round of the new era. Straight out of the box.

Luck, and what you do with it

It is fair to say the Delta was in the right place at the right moment. It is not fair to stop there. Lancia had the compact AWD turbo car and the deepest institutional rally knowledge in Europe — the Fulvia, the Stratos, the 037, the S4, plus the Fiat 124 and 131 programs inside the same group — and Martini's money, and a driver roster that read like a hall of fame ballot.

Other manufacturers got lucky too. None of them turned it into six straight championships.

Section 05 — The family treeFive cars, one relentless idea

The Integrale is not a model. It is a program — an eight-year argument with itself, each version fixing what the last one couldn't do.

Note what the numbers say. The 16V is the volume car — nearly 13,000 of them. The Evo I is scarce at 5,619, and the Evo II scarcer still. When people talk about Integrale prices going vertical, that ratio is most of the reason.

Section 06 — EvoluzioneThe one everybody pictures

Say "Delta Integrale" out loud and the image that appears in your head is the Evo. Frankfurt, September 1991; production from October. Italian enthusiasts call it the Deltona — roughly, the Big Delta — and once you have heard that you cannot unhear it.

By 1991 Group A had turned into an arms race. Toyota, Mitsubishi, Subaru and Ford were all building increasingly specialized homologation cars, and the 16V had run out of road: it could not fit bigger competition wheels, its front suspension geometry was compromised by mounting points inherited from a 1979 hatchback, and it needed more cooling and more brake than the shell would allow.

So Lancia widened everything.

What the Evo actually got

Wider front and rear tracks with wheel arches to cover them. Raised and reinforced front strut mounting points — that one is the important one, because it fixed the camber behavior that had been holding the car back since 1979. A front strut brace. Revised rear geometry. Longer suspension travel. Brembo four-piston fixed calipers on larger vented front discs, with Bosch ABS. Extra air intakes in the nose, vents in the hood, vents in the front fenders, and a cooler for the power-steering fluid. Deeper side skirts. And the adjustable roof spoiler, which on the competition car managed high-speed airflow and on the road car became the single most recognizable thing about it.

Lancia claimed the Evo could cover a rally stage roughly five to six percent faster than the 16V. In competition terms that is not an improvement, that is a different car.

Five-speed manual, always. Left-hand drive, always — Lancia never built a right-hand-drive Integrale, which is why every UK car is a personal import and why the British enthusiast scene is the way it is. Options were essentially leather and a sunroof.

Section 07 — The drivelineHow it actually puts power down

This is the heart of it, and it is worth being precise, because "all-wheel drive" in 1991 meant something completely different from what it means now.

There is no computer here. No clutch pack sampling a dozen sensors two hundred times a second, no torque vectoring, no yaw model. Everything the Integrale does, it does with gears, oil and physics — and that is exactly why it feels the way it feels.

Trazione Integrale — torque flow

Transverse engine · epicyclic center differential · Ferguson viscous coupling · Torsen rear

Nominal split, everything gripping: roughly 47 percent of torque forward, 53 percent rearward. The mild rear bias is what stops the car from feeling like a front-driver being dragged along by its nose.

The center differential

An epicyclic — planetary — gearset sets the baseline division of torque between the axles. On the 16V and every Evo, that baseline is roughly 47 percent front and 53 percent rear. Mild rear bias. Not rear-wheel drive, but enough to change the car's manners fundamentally: the rear axle is helping to push rather than merely being towed.

The Ferguson viscous coupling

Closely spaced plates sit in silicone fluid, alternating between the two sides of the driveline. When the front and rear axles turn at the same speed, nothing happens and the coupling is effectively invisible. When they diverge — a front wheel spinning up on gravel, say — the plates shear the fluid, the fluid heats, its resistance climbs, and the coupling starts fighting the difference. Torque migrates to the axle that still has grip.

The key word is reacts. It does not predict. There is a small, honest delay while physics catches up, and learning to work with that delay rather than against it is most of what makes an Integrale driver good.

The Torsen rear

Torsen is short for torque-sensing. Worm gears inside the rear differential generate internal friction proportional to load, biasing torque toward whichever rear wheel has more usable traction. It is not a clutch-pack limited-slip. Its one weakness is that it needs some resistance at both outputs to generate bias — lift a rear wheel entirely off the ground and it has nothing to push against.

What four-wheel drive does and doesn't do

It deploys power. It does not create corner-entry grip. Arrive too fast and the Integrale will understeer at you like any other nose-heavy car, and no amount of Martini striping will help. The technique — brake in a straight line, set the nose, then feed power in and let the driveline drag you out — is the whole art of the car.

What it buys you is the confidence to use everything, everywhere, in any weather. That is a different and better thing than raw grip.

Section 08 — Behind the wheelThe ravioli problem

You get in and the first surprise is that it does not feel like a race car. It feels like a nice Italian car from 1991 that happens to be very tightly wound.

The seats are the thing everyone mentions first and they deserve it. Anatomical Recaros, and they hold you the way ravioli holds its filling — sculpted so completely around you that after four hours you get out without the low-grade ache a modern sport seat leaves behind. The Momo leather wheel sits close. The gauges are exactly an arm's length away, laid out with a color-coded scheme so the dial you need reads instantly. The driving position is unapologetically driver-first.

Because the shell is a 1979 family hatchback, the glass is upright, the roof is high, and the visibility is superb — a genuinely underrated advantage over every modern performance car with its gunslit windows and its reversing camera. You can see out of an Integrale. You always know where its corners are, which matters a great deal when the corners are that far outboard.

The engine

Below boost it is unremarkable: a decent 2.0-liter four hauling a fair amount of driveline around. Then somewhere north of 2,500 rpm the turbo wakes up, the midrange arrives in a hard shove, and the car starts gathering speed far more urgently than 215 horsepower has any business doing. The Evo I does this abruptly, almost rudely. The Evo II — with its Marelli management, knock sensing and closed-loop boost control — does it progressively, which is either the improvement or the loss depending on who you ask.

The balance

On a neutral throttle the car feels secure and mildly front-led. Feed power in mid-corner and the rear bias plus the Torsen start rotating it outward and forward at the same time. Add left-foot braking or a deliberate lift and it will genuinely move around underneath you. The heroic WRC footage is not a lie, but it is also not the default: a road Evo does not powerslide out of every junction the way a rear-drive Escort will. You have to ask.

The ride

Here is the thing nobody expects. It rides well. Rallying rewards grip on broken surfaces, not stiffness, so a healthy standard Evo is firm and controlled and mechanically busy but never brutal — more compliant than a great many modern cars on 20-inch wheels. If you have driven one that hammered you, you drove one with cheap coilovers, dead dampers, or four inches missing from its ride height.

So when you are not doing 80 down a sea-cliff road or a back road in Maine with a canopy of trees and more dips and bends than a backup dancer, about to take a hard-medium right — maybe — you are wrapped in something genuinely, quietly lovely.It is not a Bentley. You will be just fine.

The Delta's ledger

1987 Juha Kankkunen · 1988 Miki Biasion · 1989 Miki Biasion · 1991 Juha Kankkunen. Lancia also finally won the Safari — the event that had humiliated European teams for decades — with the Delta in 1988, then did it again in 1989. Across its whole history Lancia holds more manufacturers' titles than any other marque in the championship: ten by the usual count, eleven if you include the 1972 season, which is exactly what Lancia's own 1991 brochure does.

The strange, perfect ending: 1992

Lancia announced its withdrawal from works rallying at the end of 1991, at the top, having just won both titles. And then the Evo went out in 1992 anyway — run by the independent Jolly Club under Claudio Bortoletto, in Martini colors, with factory-developed cars and most of the factory's brains still attached. Auriol, Kankkunen and Andrea Aghini drove, with Philippe Bugalski and Jorge Recalde on selected rounds.

Didier Auriol won six rallies that season — Monte Carlo, Corsica, the Acropolis, Argentina, the 1000 Lakes and Australia — which was the most any driver had managed in a single WRC year, and stood as the record until Sébastien Loeb broke it in 2005. He did not win the championship. Outside those six wins his results collapsed, he retired from the season-closing RAC, and Carlos Sainz's relentlessly consistent Toyota took the title by attrition.

The 1000 Lakes win is the one the brochure brags about, and it earned the bragging: Finland's fastest event had been a Scandinavian fortress for four decades, and Auriol was only the second non-Scandinavian ever to break it — Sainz had done it first, in 1990. The brochure also spells his name "Dider." Nobody proofread it. Nobody has ever cared.

The Delta took the manufacturers' title regardless. Sixth in a row, won by a privateer team, for a factory that had already left the sport.

Look at what that table says. The 205 GTI and the Mk2 Golf are the light, cheap, joyful end of the hobby and there is nothing wrong with being those things. But the Integrale is playing a different sport, and — this is the part that decides it — every single AWD turbo car below it on that list arrived after the Delta had already proven the formula.

Compact production body, turbocharged two-liter, permanent four-wheel drive, clever differentials, continuous homologation. Subaru and Mitsubishi refined that recipe for two decades. Lancia wrote it.The whole modern rally-bred hot hatch, in one line

Every special-edition Evo II carries a numbered plaque on the center console. Every one of them has also been faked, because the gap between an ordinary Evo II and a documented Giallo Ginestra is now worth more than most people's cars. Badges authenticate nothing. Chassis records authenticate everything.

The Evo III that Lancia said no to

After series production ended, Maggiora — the body specialist that had actually been building the later Evos — put together a proposal known as the Evo III, or the Viola for its purple paint: further engine-management work, more power, revised wheels and trim, some chassis refinement. It was a demonstration of where the Integrale could go next.

Lancia declined. The shell was fifteen years old, Fiat's priorities had moved, and there was no rally program left to homologate anything for. So the most successful rally car of all time simply stopped, and the Subaru Impreza inherited the world.

So: buy one in Europe and bring it home?

Every Integrale ever built is now comfortably past the 25-year threshold, which means no EPA modifications, no DOT compliance work, no Registered Importer, and no Section 232 tariff. You file an EPA 3520-1 and a DOT HS-7, tick the exemption boxes, and you are done. This is the easy end of importing.

Here is the whole math on a good, honest, documented Evo II bought in Italy at €95,000, landed in a driveway in Los Angeles.

The number that could move — read this part

US tariff policy on imported vehicles has been unusually volatile through 2026. The 25-year classic exemption from the Section 232 auto tariff is holding, but the Section 122 surcharge that expired in July has a Section 301 replacement whose country list is still being worked out. Some brokers are currently quoting EU-origin classics at roughly 12.5% all-in rather than the historic 2.5%.

If that applies to your car, add about $10,800 and the number becomes $142,400. Get a written quote from a licensed customs broker before you wire anything. This is not a place to assume.

The unromantic conclusion

Roughly $132,000 to import a €95,000 Italian car. Meanwhile Evo IIs are sitting in the United States, already imported, already titled, at asking prices between $99,000 and $159,500, with a $139,000 result on Bring a Trailer in May and a $94,001 result last September.

Which means the import play only wins if you find a genuinely cheap European car — and cheap European Integrales are cheap for reasons that will cost you more than the shipping. Buy the sorted one that is already here, unless what you want specifically is a documented special edition, in which case Europe is where they live and you should go get one.

And if you want the smart money

Buy an 8-valve Integrale at $26,000. Same architecture, same driveline philosophy, same family, 90 percent of the experience, and it is the version that was actually winning championships in 1988 and 1989. The Evo is the icon. The 8V is the bargain of the entire nineties collector market and I do not think that lasts.

Section 13 — What to checkBecause they are all over thirty now

Condition beats mileage, decisively. In rough order of what will hurt you most:

Rust and structure. Roof seams and gutters, windshield surround, front and rear strut towers, chassis rails, inner and outer sills, jacking points, floorpan, rear arches, rear suspension mounting areas, tailgate, door bottoms, fuel-tank area. The wide arches hide repairs beautifully, which is precisely the problem.

Cracking and fatigue. Front strut-tower area, strut-brace mounts, suspension pickup points, steering-rack mountings, engine and gearbox mounts. Aggressive springs and solid bushings accelerate all of it in a shell this age.

Engine. Timing-belt age matters more than timing-belt mileage — service on the calendar. Then the balance-shaft belt and tensioners, water pump, oil pressure, turbo wear, crankcase breathing, head gasket, cooling-system corrosion, injectors. Be extremely suspicious of ECU modifications and any car running more boost than 1.0 bar without supporting work.

Driveline. Noise from the center or rear diff, propshaft vibration, worn CV and universal joints, transfer-case leaks, a tired viscous coupling, Torsen wear, wrong lubricants. And tires: all four must match in brand, model, size, tread depth and pressure. Persistent rolling-circumference differences make the driveline absorb a speed difference continuously, forever, until something expensive gives up.

Authenticity. High values breed reconstruction. A "real Evo" may be an earlier Integrale wearing Evo panels, a standard Delta dressed up, a replacement shell carrying another car's identity, or a rebuild from three donors. Verify chassis number, stamped body number, factory build records, original market specification, homologation-correct body details, weld and seam integrity, paint depth. Hire someone who knows Integrales specifically — not a general classic inspector.

The verdict

The Integrale is the only hot hatch that ever had to prove itself against the entire world, every weekend, for six consecutive years, on every surface there is. It won. Then it stopped, and nothing has been allowed to be that car since — because homologation rules changed, because crash structures changed, because no manufacturer will ever again build five thousand road cars purely so a rally team can have the parts it wants. The Golf GTI is the king of a category. The Delta Integrale is the king of the argument.

Section 14 — The endingWhy there will never be another one

This is worth being precise about, because "they don't make them like that anymore" is usually lazy. Here it is literally true, for four specific reasons.

Group A is gone. The whole point of the Integrale was that the FIA forced Lancia to sell you the parts. Five thousand road cars, or the rally car is illegal. World Rally Car rules replaced that in 1997 and severed the link entirely: a modern rally car shares a silhouette with its showroom counterpart and almost nothing else. Nobody has to sell you anything anymore.

The shell could not exist today. A 1979 monocoque with strut towers moved outward and mounting points relocated would not survive five minutes of modern crash regulation. The Evo's entire engineering approach — take an old production shell and modify it until it works — is now illegal in every market that matters.

The economics inverted. Lancia built 44,296 Integrales because Group A demanded volume. A manufacturer building a homologation special today builds 500 of them at four times the price, because there is no rule forcing otherwise and the margin is better.

And Lancia, essentially, stopped. The brand shrank to a single model sold in a single country for the better part of a decade. It is being revived now, with an HF badge and a little red elephant back on the fender, and I hope it works. But the company that could put six consecutive world championships on a family hatchback does not exist in that form anymore.

What is left is 44,296 cars, most of them rusted or crashed or driven into the ground by people who did not know what they had. The survivors are the last physical evidence of a thing that cannot happen twice: an ordinary five-door hatchback, forced to evolve year after year by a rulebook, until it became the most successful rally car ever made.

I saw one in Hong Kong in 1996 and I have not stopped thinking about it since. That is not nostalgia. That is just the correct reaction to the best hot hatch anyone ever built.

Fact-check notes

Evo II production. Sources split badly: roughly 4,223 by one count, about 2,481 by another. Total Integrale production of 44,296 is the widely agreed figure, and 24 of those went to Zagato to become the Hyena.

Power figures. 210 and 215 are the standard Evo I and Evo II numbers, but you will see 200, 210, 212 and 215 for the same cars depending on whether a source is quoting PS, bhp, CV or SAE net, and whether the car has a catalyst. The period collector card quoting "210 bhp at 5,750 rpm" and a $33,395 original price is describing an Evo I, and that price is a conversion — the Integrale was never officially sold new in the United States.

That same card lists production as "approximately 25,000." It is out by more than 19,000 cars. It also gives a current value of $20,000 to $30,000, which tells you rather a lot about when it was printed.

The 1991 brochure claims 215 bhp for a car sold in 1991. That figure belongs to the Evo II from 1993; period marketing copy was routinely generous. The same brochure spells Didier Auriol's name "Dider."

Homologation. The FIA lists the later Integrale under Group A number 5448, effective 2 January 1992. The database shows an adjusted capacity of about 3,392 cc — that is the FIA's turbocharged-engine equivalency multiplier applied to 1,995 cc, not a secret 3.4-liter engine.

Market data caution. CLASSIC.COM currently reports an "average sale price" of $232,082 for the Evo II. That figure is corrupted by at least one Japanese auction result recorded as ¥9,102,000 and read as dollars — the car actually sold for roughly $59,000. We have used the site's Market Benchmark and individual verified results instead, and we would suggest you do the same.

The little red elephant

Two badges sit on the nose of every car in this story, and neither one means what people assume. HF is not a model designation — it stands for High Fidelity, and it began in 1960 with a club for customers loyal enough to have bought six new Lancias. Fidelity to the marque, not to the engine.

The elephant came from somewhere else entirely. The HF letters first appeared in 1961 on the Pininfarina Flaminia coupé, then the Flaminia Sport Zagato, then the Flavia. The elephant — trunk stretched forward, which in Eastern tradition is a symbol of victory — did not meet those letters until 1966, on the Fulvia coupé. Together they became the official mark of Lancia's sports cars, ran through the Stratos until 1978, and then went to sleep for thirteen years.

Lancia's own 1991 brochure describes what happened next better than we could: the new Delta HF integrale had roused the little red elephant from its slumbers, and taken it out for its greatest race.

That story is too good to bury at the bottom of somebody else's article, so it is getting its own. The Little Red Elephant →
